accuracy.evidence: Purpose categories (persuade, inform, entertain) and the own-view versus author's-view distinction match CCSS RI.2.6 and RI.3.6 and the KS2 programme of study (fact versus opinion, how language contributes to meaning). Push-word cues (imperatives, should, must, superlatives) follow standard persuasive-language features; every lab text was checked: sharks have cartilage skeletons, the Great Fire of 1666 began in a bakery, burned about four days and destroyed roughly 13,200 houses (given as about 13,000).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips for author's purpose: any text with facts must inform (the 9 am fact and the '6 out of 10 kids' items), fun or colourful means entertain even when selling (WHY table and 'fun' feedback), disagreeing means you misread (view-line prediction and 'wrong' feedback), and naming a purpose without textual proof (Prove it step and 'feel'/'count' feedback).

lab_distinct.evidence: Five mechanics built for this standard: a three-tray purpose deal with a slip message for each of the six wrong tray pairs, a tap-the-push-word passage laid out as word chips, a two-pin author/me view line, a two-slot loaded-word swapper driving an attitude meter, and a name-then-prove step. Passed the 30% shingle gate; flagauth (word choice in stories) and flagbook (book parts, point and reasons) share none of these mechanics.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner sorts first and is corrected with the reason, then discovers that a persuasive advert can contain a fact while push words reveal its purpose, then sees on the view line that their pin can sit away from the author's, then hears the attitude flip from neutral to for to against by changing one word, and finally does the full reading move of naming a purpose and quoting the line that proves it.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions each with a tempting wrong option the lab then settles: 'Come to Funland' as inform (it lands in Persuade), 'a fact means inform' (the advert with 9 am is persuading), 'disagreeing means you read it wrong' (the pins sit apart and the lab says that is fine), and 'a fact is a fact' (the meter swings with one word).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions with twelve distinct m= messages naming the slip: treating a selling fact as information, fun as entertainment, true facts as a story, a noun or a day as a push word, disagreeing as misreading, expecting the author to change, misreading 'wasted', claiming attitude cannot be told, and using feelings or counting instead of textual proof.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and everyday examples (adverts, owls, wasted versus spent money) and passed the learner kid limit; adult text names the standards and is within the 9.5 target. Canvas prompts are under twelve words; every button is one emoji plus one or two words.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and the 12% duplicate gate. Each kid paragraph does one job (purpose, persuade cues, inform and entertain, point of view with attitude); adult paragraphs cover standards, PIE and language cues, named mistakes, and the attitude routine; the family tip is a single cereal-box activity.

mobile.evidence: Checked screenshots at 360 px (light) and iPhone 13 (dark) for all six steps: trays, word chips, view line, swap slots and prove buttons fit inside the canvas with nothing clipped; word chips wrap by measured width; the canvas grows taller on narrow screens (tall 1.25).

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, every task completed via Show me, no console errors. Every drag or tap has a button route (tray buttons, one button per word, pin arrow buttons, swap buttons, purpose and sentence buttons); the canvas aria-label reports the current text, words found, both pin positions, the sentence and attitude.

sources: Common Core State Standards for ELA, Reading: Informational Text RI.2.6 and RI.3.6
Department for Education (2013), English programmes of study: key stages 1 and 2, Years 3-6 reading comprehension (fact and opinion; language, structure and presentation)
Museum of London: The Great Fire of London 1666 (start in Thomas Farriner's bakery, four days, about 13,200 houses)
Natural History Museum: shark skeletons are made of cartilage
